supportingEvidence.title: Reuters: refiners and energy major plan to avoid Iran-blacklisted vessels
supportingEvidence.note: Four sources with direct knowledge say at least three Indian refiners and one global energy major plan to stop using blacklisted vessels, including for ship-to-ship transfers. This is observed counterparty behavior rather than only policy rhetoric.

supportingEvidence.title: Argus Media: PGSA blacklist raises freight-market concerns
supportingEvidence.note: Independent freight-market reporting says the PGSA rule can propagate risk beyond the originally listed ships through STS and transshipment links, potentially reducing willing counterparties.

supportingEvidence.title: Tasnim: PGSA blacklist and STS-contagion warning
supportingEvidence.note: Iranian reporting reproduces the authority's warning that vessels conducting ship-to-ship operations with listed ships may themselves risk being blacklisted.

contradictingEvidence.title: Reuters: likely substitution rather than complete trade stoppage
contradictingEvidence.note: Industry participants expect operators to shift toward alternative vessels or routes rather than halt Gulf crude trade entirely; the blacklist may reroute flows more than reduce aggregate supply.

contradictingEvidence.title: Reuters: oil markets still price reopening optimism
contradictingEvidence.note: Crude prices are declining on Iran-Oman reopening talks, implying the market currently expects logistical substitution and diplomacy to outweigh at least part of the blacklist risk.

falsifier: Downgrade the behavioral-contagion thesis if blacklisted vessels and their STS counterparties continue receiving comparable chartering activity to matched non-listed vessels, no measurable route/ownership/AIS changes occur, and freight or insurance premia do not differentiate despite the blacklist.

title: Iran's Hormuz blacklist begins changing real chartering behavior
summary: Iran's vessel blacklist has moved from a threat into observable counterparty behavior: multiple refiners and a global energy major plan to avoid listed ships and STS interactions with them, validating network-contagion risk while leaving aggregate supply effects uncertain.
delta: Upgrade the Hormuz permission-regime model from announced blacklist risk to observed behavioral propagation. Keep aggregate supply impact unresolved: the first effect is counterparty substitution, due diligence and routing changes, not proven net supply loss.
firstOrderImpacts: reduced charter demand for listed vessels
greater due-diligence and counterparty screening around STS transfers
possible redistribution of freight and insurance premia toward exposed vessel networks
secondOrderImpacts: network effects may propagate sanctions-like behavior without formal legal sanctions from the buyers' home jurisdictions
vessel ownership, STS counterparties and AIS behavior become higher-value predictors than simple throughput counts
market-wide oil supply may remain resilient if substitution is fast, creating a divergence between network stress and headline crude prices

alphaHunter.hypothesis: Blacklist-network adjacency will predict charter avoidance, route changes and risk-premium differentiation earlier than aggregate Hormuz traffic or oil-price headlines alone.
alphaHunter.baseline: PGSA blacklist announcement plus aggregate Hormuz vessel counts and Brent price action
alphaHunter.alternativeData: vessel identity/ownership, STS counterparty graph, chartering changes, AIS-dark behavior, freight differentials and war-risk insurance for listed versus matched unlisted vessels
alphaHunter.incrementalValueMetric: 3-7 day difference in charter activity, route changes and risk-premium movement for listed/adjacent vessels versus a matched unlisted cohort, plus forecast error relative to the aggregate baseline
alphaHunter.killCondition: Kill the graph-expansion hypothesis if blacklist adjacency fails to produce measurable out-of-sample differences in chartering, routing, freight or insurance after controlling for vessel class and Gulf exposure.
